body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

The laboratory findings in disseminated intravascular coagulopathy include ...

A. prolonged APTT.
B. shortened PT.
C. low vWF.
D. low platelet.
answer:
| Option | T/F | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A. prolonged APTT. | **T** | Consumption of clotting factors. |
| B. shortened PT. | **F** | PT is **prolonged**. |
| C. low vWF. | **F** | vWF is usually normal or raised (endothelial activation). |
| D. low platelet. | **T** | Platelets are consumed. |

> [!answer]
> **A T, B F, C F, D T**
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

DIC = systemic activation of coagulation with consumption of **platelets** and **factors** (fibrinogen, V, VIII) and secondary fibrinolysis: **prolonged PT, APTT, TT**, **low fibrinogen**, **thrombocytopenia**, **raised D-dimer/FDPs**, schistocytes. vWF is released from damaged endothelium and is not typically low.

## Simplified explanation

In DIC, clotting factors and platelets are used up, so PT and APTT lengthen and platelets fall.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

The laboratory findings in haemorrhagic disease of the new born includes ...

A. prolonged APTT.
B. prolonged PT.
C. low fibrinogen.
D. low platelet count.
answer:
| Option | T/F | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A. prolonged APTT. | **T** | Factor IX and X deficiency. |
| B. prolonged PT. | **T** | Factor VII, X and II deficiency. |
| C. low fibrinogen. | **F** | Fibrinogen is not vitamin K-dependent. |
| D. low platelet count. | **F** | Platelets are normal. |

> [!answer]
> **A T, B T, C F, D F**
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**Haemorrhagic disease of the newborn (vitamin K deficiency bleeding)**: deficiency of vitamin K-dependent factors **II, VII, IX, X** → **prolonged PT** (most sensitive) and **APTT**, normal TT, fibrinogen and platelets. Prevented by vitamin K at birth.

## Simplified explanation

Low vitamin K lowers factors II, VII, IX and X, so PT and APTT are long; fibrinogen and platelets are normal.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

The laboratory findings in disseminated intravascular coagulopathy include ...

A. prolonged TT.
B. low fibrin degradation products.
C. low fibrinogen levels.
D. increased D-dimers.
answer:
| Option | T/F | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A. prolonged TT. | **T** | Low fibrinogen and FDPs prolong TT. |
| B. low fibrin degradation products. | **F** | FDPs are **raised**. |
| C. low fibrinogen levels. | **T** | Fibrinogen is consumed. |
| D. increased D-dimers. | **T** | Cross-linked fibrin is lysed. |

> [!answer]
> **A T, B F, C T, D T**
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

In DIC the thrombin time is prolonged by hypofibrinogenaemia and by FDPs, which inhibit fibrin polymerisation. **D-dimer** and FDPs are high; fibrinogen is low (may be normal early because it is an acute-phase protein).

## Simplified explanation

DIC uses up fibrinogen and creates lots of fibrin breakdown products (D-dimers), which lengthen the thrombin time.
hint: Clot made and broken down at the same time.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

Causes of disseminated intravascular coagulopathy includes ...

A. septic abortion.
B. vascular aneurysms.
C. severe *Plasmodium falciparum* infection.
D. amniotic fluid embolism.
answer:
| Option | T/F | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A. septic abortion. | **T** | Sepsis plus release of tissue factor. |
| B. vascular aneurysms. | **T** | Large aneurysms/vascular malformations cause localised consumption and chronic DIC. |
| C. severe *Plasmodium falciparum* infection. | **T** | Severe malaria can trigger DIC. |
| D. amniotic fluid embolism. | **T** | Classic obstetric cause. |

> [!answer]
> **A T, B T, C T, D T**
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Causes of DIC: **sepsis** (Gram-negative, meningococcal, **falciparum malaria**), **obstetric** (abruption, **amniotic fluid embolism**, **septic abortion**, retained dead fetus), malignancy (APL, adenocarcinoma), trauma/burns, snake bite, incompatible transfusion, **vascular abnormalities** (aortic aneurysm, Kasabach-Merritt haemangioma), liver failure.

## Simplified explanation

All four can set off widespread clotting and cause DIC.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

The cause(s) of haemorrhagic disease of the new born include ...

A. immaturity of the renal tubules.
B. lack of gastrointestinal tract microbiota.
C. low level of factor VIII.
D. sex-linked inheritance.
answer:
| Option | T/F | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A. immaturity of the renal tubules. | **F** | Not related. |
| B. lack of gastrointestinal tract microbiota. | **T** | Gut bacteria that synthesise vitamin K₂ are absent at birth. |
| C. low level of factor VIII. | **F** | FVIII is not vitamin K-dependent; levels are near adult values. |
| D. sex-linked inheritance. | **F** | It is acquired, not inherited. |

> [!answer]
> **A F, B T, C F, D F**
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Newborn vitamin K deficiency arises from poor placental transfer, **sterile gut**, low vitamin K in **breast milk** and immature hepatic function; risk rises with maternal anticonvulsants/warfarin and cholestasis.

## Simplified explanation

Newborns have no gut bacteria to make vitamin K and get little from breast milk.
hint: Where does part of our vitamin K come from?

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

Vitamin K deficiency leads to ...

A. low levels of factor III.
B. low level of factor VIII.
C. shortened APTT.
D. shortened PT.
answer:
| Option | T/F | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A. low levels of factor III. | **F** | Factor III (tissue factor) is not vitamin K-dependent. |
| B. low level of factor VIII. | **F** | Not vitamin K-dependent. |
| C. shortened APTT. | **F** | APTT is **prolonged**. |
| D. shortened PT. | **F** | PT is **prolonged**. |

> [!answer]
> **A F, B F, C F, D F**
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Vitamin K is the cofactor for **γ-glutamyl carboxylase**, which carboxylates factors **II, VII, IX, X** and proteins **C, S, Z**. Deficiency (or warfarin) produces non-functional PIVKAs → **prolonged PT** and APTT.

## Simplified explanation

Vitamin K deficiency lowers II, VII, IX and X, so clotting times get longer, not shorter. All four are false.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

Liver diseases may affect the haemostatic function through ...

A. reduced thrombopoietin production.
B. Dysfibrinogenaemia.
C. reduced factor VIII levels.
D. reduced factor III levels.
answer:
| Option | T/F | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A. reduced thrombopoietin production. | **T** | TPO is made in the liver; low TPO → thrombocytopenia. |
| B. Dysfibrinogenaemia. | **T** | Abnormally sialylated fibrinogen. |
| C. reduced factor VIII levels. | **F** | FVIII is made by sinusoidal endothelium and is normal or **raised**. |
| D. reduced factor III levels. | **F** | Tissue factor is not a liver product. |

> [!answer]
> **A T, B T, C F, D F**
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Liver disease: reduced synthesis of factors (II, V, VII, IX, X, XI, fibrinogen) and anticoagulants (AT, protein C/S), **acquired dysfibrinogenaemia**, **thrombocytopenia** (reduced TPO, hypersplenism), hyperfibrinolysis, vitamin K malabsorption in cholestasis. **FVIII and vWF are raised**.

## Simplified explanation

The liver makes TPO and fibrinogen, so liver disease lowers platelets and gives abnormal fibrinogen. FVIII goes up, not down.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

Disseminated intravascular coagulopathy is characterised by ...

A. generalized thrombosis.
B. generalized bleeding.
C. thrombocytopenia.
D. excessive fibrinolysis.
answer:
| Option | T/F | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A. generalized thrombosis. | **T** | Widespread microvascular thrombi. |
| B. generalized bleeding. | **T** | Consumption of factors/platelets. |
| C. thrombocytopenia. | **T** | Consumption. |
| D. excessive fibrinolysis. | **T** | Secondary fibrinolysis (high D-dimer). |

> [!answer]
> **A T, B T, C T, D T**
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

DIC combines **microvascular thrombosis** (organ failure) with **bleeding** from consumption of platelets and factors and from **secondary fibrinolysis**. The balance varies: hyperfibrinolytic in APL/obstetric DIC, thrombotic in sepsis.

## Simplified explanation

DIC causes clots and bleeding everywhere at once, with low platelets and lots of clot breakdown.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

Lupus anticoagulant ...

A. inhibits carbohydrate moiety-dependent reactions.
B. shortens APTT.
C. is associated with bleeding.
D. causes haemorrhagic disease of the newborn.
answer:
| Option | T/F | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A. inhibits carbohydrate moiety-dependent reactions. | **F** | It interferes with **phospholipid-dependent** reactions. |
| B. shortens APTT. | **F** | It **prolongs** the APTT in vitro. |
| C. is associated with bleeding. | **F** | Associated with **thrombosis**. |
| D. causes haemorrhagic disease of the newborn. | **F** | Associated with recurrent fetal loss, not newborn bleeding. |

> [!answer]
> **A F, B F, C F, D F**
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**Lupus anticoagulant** = antibodies (to β2-glycoprotein I/prothrombin–phospholipid complexes) that prolong phospholipid-dependent tests (APTT, dRVVT) in vitro without correction on mixing, but cause **thrombosis** and pregnancy morbidity in vivo.

## Simplified explanation

Lupus anticoagulant lengthens lab clotting times by blocking phospholipid, but in the body it causes clots and miscarriages. All four are false.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

Activated protein C resistance ...

A. is caused by resistance of factor VIIa to degradation.
B. is associated with arterial bleeding.
C. is a sex-linked disorder.
D. causes shortened APTT.
answer:
| Option | T/F | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A. is caused by resistance of factor VIIa to degradation. | **F** | It is resistance of **factor Va** (factor V Leiden, R506Q). |
| B. is associated with arterial bleeding. | **F** | Associated with **venous thrombosis**. |
| C. is a sex-linked disorder. | **F** | Autosomal (chromosome 1). |
| D. causes shortened APTT. | **F** | Baseline APTT is normal; the APC-resistance test shows reduced prolongation with APC. |

> [!answer]
> **A F, B F, C F, D F**
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**APC resistance** is mostly due to **factor V Leiden** (F5 R506Q), autosomal dominant, which makes factor Va resistant to cleavage by activated protein C; it causes **venous thromboembolism**. Test: APTT ratio with/without APC, confirmed by genotyping.

## Simplified explanation

APC resistance is factor V Leiden: factor Va resists breakdown, causing vein clots. All statements are wrong.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

Biliary tract obstruction may cause ...

A. increased absorption of vitamin K from the gastrointestinal tract.
B. decreased production of factor II.
C. decreased production of factor VIII.
D. increased production of fibrin degradation products.
answer:
| Option | T/F | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A. increased absorption of vitamin K from the gastrointestinal tract. | **F** | Lack of bile salts **reduces** fat-soluble vitamin K absorption. |
| B. decreased production of factor II. | **T** | Vitamin K-dependent factor. |
| C. decreased production of factor VIII. | **F** | Not vitamin K-dependent. |
| D. increased production of fibrin degradation products. | **F** | Not a feature of cholestasis. |

> [!answer]
> **A F, B T, C F, D F**
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Obstructive jaundice → no bile salts in the gut → malabsorption of fat-soluble **vitamin K** → reduced functional **II, VII, IX, X** → prolonged PT, corrected by parenteral vitamin K (unlike hepatocellular disease).

## Simplified explanation

No bile means vitamin K isn't absorbed, so factor II (and VII, IX, X) fall.
hint: Bile is needed to absorb fat-soluble vitamins.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

Increased peripheral blood fibrin degradation products ...

A. causes impaired platelet aggregation.
B. increases thrombin activation.
C. activates clot retraction.
D. is characteristic of haemophilia a disease.
answer:
| Option | T/F | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A. causes impaired platelet aggregation. | **T** | FDPs coat platelets and interfere with aggregation. |
| B. increases thrombin activation. | **F** | FDPs have **antithrombin** activity. |
| C. activates clot retraction. | **F** | They impair fibrin polymerisation and clot formation. |
| D. is characteristic of haemophilia a disease. | **F** | Haemophilia has normal FDPs. |

> [!answer]
> **A T, B F, C F, D F**
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

FDPs (fragments X, Y, D, E) **inhibit thrombin**, interfere with **fibrin polymerisation** and **impair platelet function**, aggravating bleeding in DIC and hyperfibrinolysis.

## Simplified explanation

Fibrin breakdown products act as anticoagulants: they block thrombin and stop platelets clumping.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

The peripheral blood film of an individual suffering from a disseminated intravascular coagulopathy may show ...

A. red cell fragmentation.
B. schistocyte.
C. hypochromic red cells.
D. Pappenheimer granules in red cells.
answer:
| Option | T/F | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A. red cell fragmentation. | **T** | Microangiopathic haemolysis. |
| B. schistocyte. | **T** | Fragmented red cells. |
| C. hypochromic red cells. | **F** | Not a feature of DIC. |
| D. Pappenheimer granules in red cells. | **F** | Iron granules (sideroblastic anaemia, hyposplenism). |

> [!answer]
> **A T, B T, C F, D F**
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Fibrin strands in small vessels shear red cells, producing **schistocytes**, helmet cells and microspherocytes (microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia), with **thrombocytopenia**.

## Simplified explanation

Red cells are chopped by fibrin strands, so fragments (schistocytes) appear.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

Lack of -------------- in a client may be an indication that his thrombophilia is caused by paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria.

A. CD55
B. CD59
C. protein C
D. antithrombin III
answer:
| Option | T/F | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A. CD55 | **T** | GPI-anchored complement regulator absent in PNH. |
| B. CD59 | **T** | GPI-anchored complement regulator absent in PNH. |
| C. protein C | **F** | Protein C deficiency is a separate thrombophilia. |
| D. antithrombin III | **F** | A separate thrombophilia. |

> [!answer]
> **A T, B T, C F, D F**
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

PNH, diagnosed by flow cytometry showing loss of **CD55/CD59** on red cells (and FLAER/CD24/CD14 on white cells), is an important acquired cause of thrombosis at unusual sites (hepatic, portal, cerebral veins).

## Simplified explanation

PNH cells lack CD55 and CD59.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

In lupus anticoagulant disease, ...

A. there is prolonged APTT which corrects with 1:1 mix with normal plasma.
B. there is shortened thrombin time which corrects with 1:1 mix with normal plasma.
C. there is low platelet count as a result of autoantibodies against MHC I antigens.
D. there is paraproteinaemia due to deranged IgG production.
answer:
| Option | T/F | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A. there is prolonged APTT which corrects with 1:1 mix with normal plasma. | **F** | It **does not correct** (inhibitor). |
| B. there is shortened thrombin time which corrects with 1:1 mix with normal plasma. | **F** | TT is usually normal. |
| C. there is low platelet count as a result of autoantibodies against MHC I antigens. | **F** | Mild thrombocytopenia may occur, but not via anti-MHC I antibodies. |
| D. there is paraproteinaemia due to deranged IgG production. | **F** | LA is a polyclonal autoantibody, not a paraprotein. |

> [!answer]
> **A F, B F, C F, D F**
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

LA screening: prolonged APTT/dRVVT that **fails to correct on 1:1 mixing** and **corrects with excess phospholipid** (confirm step). Thrombin time is normal (no phospholipid dependence).

## Simplified explanation

Lupus anticoagulant prolongs the APTT and it does not correct when mixed with normal plasma. All statements are false.
hint: An inhibitor does not correct on mixing.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

The recommended blood:citrate ratio for coagulation studies include ...

A. 2.7 ml blood to 0.3 ml sodium citrate.
B. 3.5 ml blood to 0.5 ml sodium citrate.
C. 4.7 ml blood to 0.3 ml sodium citrate.
D. 4.5 ml blood to 0.5 ml sodium citrate.
answer:
| Option | T/F | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A. 2.7 ml blood to 0.3 ml sodium citrate. | **T** | 9:1. |
| B. 3.5 ml blood to 0.5 ml sodium citrate. | **F** | 7:1. |
| C. 4.7 ml blood to 0.3 ml sodium citrate. | **F** | ≈16:1. |
| D. 4.5 ml blood to 0.5 ml sodium citrate. | **T** | 9:1. |

> [!answer]
> **A T, B F, C F, D T**
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Coagulation samples use **3.2% (0.109 M) trisodium citrate** at **9 parts blood to 1 part citrate**, e.g. 2.7 + 0.3 ml or 4.5 + 0.5 ml.

## Simplified explanation

The ratio must be 9:1: 2.7 + 0.3 and 4.5 + 0.5 are correct.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

A medical laboratory scientist [MLS] was scheduled to take blood into a standard citrated tube that has been calibrated to take 5 ml of blood. Suppose the patient has a haematocrite of 0.33, what should the MLS do? The MLS ...

A. reduce the anticoagulant in the tube.
B. increase the blood volume to correspond to the anticoagulant.
C. should take exactly 5 ml of blood into the tube.
D. should inform the clinician that the haematocrite makes the patient unfit for the requested test.
answer:
| Option | T/F | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A. reduce the anticoagulant in the tube. | **F** | Only needed when Hct >0.55. |
| B. increase the blood volume to correspond to the anticoagulant. | **F** | Not needed. |
| C. should take exactly 5 ml of blood into the tube. | **T** | Hct 0.33 needs no adjustment. |
| D. should inform the clinician that the haematocrite makes the patient unfit for the requested test. | **F** | No such restriction. |

> [!answer]
> **A F, B F, C T, D F**
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Citrate volume is adjusted only when **Hct > 0.55** (CLSI): citrate (ml) = 0.00185 × blood volume (ml) × (100 − Hct%). With Hct 0.33 the tube is filled to the mark as usual.

## Simplified explanation

A haematocrit of 0.33 is fine, so just fill the tube to the 5 ml mark.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

Platelet poor plasma (PPP) ...

A. is required for Lupus anticoagulant testing.
B. must contain ≤50 × 10⁹/L platelets.
C. is required for heparin monitoring.
D. may be stored frozen.
answer:
| Option | T/F | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A. is required for Lupus anticoagulant testing. | **T** | Residual platelets supply phospholipid and neutralise LA. |
| B. must contain ≤50 × 10⁹/L platelets. | **F** | PPP must contain **<10 × 10⁹/L** platelets. |
| C. is required for heparin monitoring. | **T** | Platelets release PF4, which neutralises heparin. |
| D. may be stored frozen. | **T** | Frozen at −70 °C (or −20 °C short term). |

> [!answer]
> **A T, B F, C T, D T**
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

PPP (platelets <10 × 10⁹/L) is made by double centrifugation (~1500–2000 g, 15 min ×2) or filtration. It is essential for **LA testing**, **heparin monitoring** and frozen storage.

## Simplified explanation

Platelet-poor plasma (<10 × 10⁹/L platelets) is needed for lupus and heparin tests and can be frozen.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

Thrombocytopenia may be caused by ...

A. vitamin B12 deficiency.
B. splenic atrophy.
C. paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria.
D. alcoholism.
answer:
| Option | T/F | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A. vitamin B12 deficiency. | **T** | Ineffective megakaryopoiesis. |
| B. splenic atrophy. | **F** | Hyposplenism causes **thrombocytosis**. |
| C. paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria. | **T** | Marrow failure component. |
| D. alcoholism. | **T** | Marrow toxicity, folate deficiency, hypersplenism. |

> [!answer]
> **A T, B F, C T, D T**
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Thrombocytopenia: **decreased production** (aplasia, PNH, megaloblastic anaemia, alcohol, infiltration), **increased destruction** (ITP, DIC, TTP, drugs), **sequestration** (hypersplenism). Splenic atrophy/splenectomy raises the count.

## Simplified explanation

B12 deficiency, PNH and alcohol lower platelets; a small or absent spleen raises them.
hint: Spleen size and platelets move oppositely.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

Thromboelastography ...

A. requires heparinized blood
B. requires citrated blood
C. requires non-anticoagulated blood
D. measures the viscoelastic properties of blood
answer:
| Option | T/F | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A. requires heparinized blood | **F** | Heparin would abolish clotting (unless heparinase cups are used). |
| B. requires citrated blood | **F** | Native or citrated (recalcified) blood can be used; citrate is not required. |
| C. requires non-anticoagulated blood | **F** | Not required; citrated samples are common. |
| D. measures the viscoelastic properties of blood | **T** | It records clot formation, strength and lysis. |

> [!answer]
> **A F, B F, C F, D T**
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**TEG/ROTEM** measure the **viscoelastic** changes of whole blood as it clots: R/CT (clotting time), K/α angle (kinetics), MA/MCF (clot strength: platelets + fibrinogen) and LY30 (fibrinolysis). Samples may be native or citrated blood recalcified at testing.

## Simplified explanation

TEG measures how the clot forms, strengthens and breaks down; it can use fresh or citrated blood.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

The laboratory findings in a normal day old baby includes ...

A. haemoglobin concentration of 13.6 g/dL.
B. reticulocyte count of 1.1%.
C. MCV of 85 fL.
D. leucocyte count of 5.5 × 10⁹/L.
answer:
| Option | T/F | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A. haemoglobin concentration of 13.6 g/dL. | **F** | Normal newborn Hb is ~14–24 g/dL (mean ~18). |
| B. reticulocyte count of 1.1%. | **F** | Neonatal reticulocytes are ~3–7%. |
| C. MCV of 85 fL. | **F** | Neonatal MCV is ~100–120 fL. |
| D. leucocyte count of 5.5 × 10⁹/L. | **F** | Neonatal WBC is ~10–26 × 10⁹/L. |

> [!answer]
> **A F, B F, C F, D F**
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Day-1 neonate: Hb ~18 (14–24) g/dL, Hct 0.45–0.65, MCV 100–120 fL, reticulocytes 3–7%, nucleated red cells present, WBC 10–26 × 10⁹/L (neutrophil predominant).

## Simplified explanation

Newborns have high Hb, big red cells, many reticulocytes and a high white count, so every value given is too low.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

Mr. Djokoto's coagulation profile showed prolongation of both APTT and PT. The laboratory scientist undertook mixing assay using 1:1 mix of Mr. Djokoto's plasma and normal plasma. In interpreting his laboratory findings ...

A. correction of both APTT and PT demonstrates the absence of coagulation factor deficiency.
B. correction of both APTT and PT demonstrate the presence of coagulation inhibitor in Mr Djokoto's plasma.
C. if both APTT and PT remain prolonged after the mixing assay, then Mr. Djokoto has deficiency of factor XIII.
D. if both APTT and PT remain prolonged after the mixing assay, then Mr. Djokoto might be suffering from vitamin K deficiency.
answer:
| Option | T/F | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A. correction of both APTT and PT demonstrates the absence of coagulation factor deficiency. | **F** | Correction indicates **factor deficiency**. |
| B. correction of both APTT and PT demonstrate the presence of coagulation inhibitor in Mr Djokoto's plasma. | **F** | An inhibitor would **prevent** correction. |
| C. if both APTT and PT remain prolonged after the mixing assay, then Mr. Djokoto has deficiency of factor XIII. | **F** | FXIII deficiency does not prolong PT or APTT. |
| D. if both APTT and PT remain prolonged after the mixing assay, then Mr. Djokoto might be suffering from vitamin K deficiency. | **F** | Vitamin K deficiency is a factor deficiency and corrects on mixing. |

> [!answer]
> **A F, B F, C F, D F**
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

In a 1:1 mix, normal plasma supplies ≥50% of each factor, enough to normalise clotting times if the patient is simply **deficient**. **Failure to correct** indicates an **inhibitor** (lupus anticoagulant, factor antibodies, heparin). FXIII deficiency gives normal PT/APTT.

## Simplified explanation

If mixing fixes the result, a factor is missing; if it doesn't, there's an inhibitor. All four statements get this wrong.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

The following clinical presentations are associated with circulating lupus anticoagulant and anticardiolipin antibodies:

A. recurrent fetal loss.
B. venous thrombosis.
C. thrombocytopenia.
D. arterial thrombosis.
answer:
| Option | T/F | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A. recurrent fetal loss. | **T** | Obstetric APS. |
| B. venous thrombosis. | **T** | The commonest thrombotic event. |
| C. thrombocytopenia. | **T** | Seen in a proportion of APS patients. |
| D. arterial thrombosis. | **T** | Stroke, MI. |

> [!answer]
> **A T, B T, C T, D T**
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**Antiphospholipid syndrome**: **venous or arterial thrombosis** and/or **pregnancy morbidity**, with persistent LA, anticardiolipin or anti-β2GPI antibodies (≥12 weeks apart). Thrombocytopenia, livedo reticularis and valve disease are associated.

## Simplified explanation

Antiphospholipid antibodies cause miscarriages, vein and artery clots, and low platelets. All four are true.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

The platelet membrane phospholipid is important in the conversion of the following coagulation factors to their active forms. Conversion of factor ...

A. X to Xa.
B. XIII to XIIIa.
C. III to IIIa.
D. II to IIa.
answer:
| Option | T/F | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A. X to Xa. | **T** | Tenase complex (IXa + VIIIa + Ca²⁺) assembles on phospholipid. |
| B. XIII to XIIIa. | **F** | Thrombin activates FXIII without a phospholipid surface. |
| C. III to IIIa. | **F** | Tissue factor (III) is not converted to an 'activated' form. |
| D. II to IIa. | **T** | Prothrombinase (Xa + Va + Ca²⁺) on phospholipid. |

> [!answer]
> **A T, B F, C F, D T**
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Activated platelets expose **phosphatidylserine**, which (with Ca²⁺) anchors γ-carboxylated factors to assemble the **tenase** (IXa/VIIIa: X→Xa) and **prothrombinase** (Xa/Va: II→IIa) complexes.

## Simplified explanation

Platelet phospholipid is the surface for the tenase (X→Xa) and prothrombinase (II→IIa) complexes.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

Bleeding time may be prolonged in ...

A. von Willebrand disease.
B. vitamin K deficiency.
C. disseminated intravascular coagulopathy.
D. antiphospholipid syndrome.
answer:
| Option | T/F | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A. von Willebrand disease. | **T** | Defective platelet adhesion. |
| B. vitamin K deficiency. | **F** | Normal in coagulation factor deficiency. |
| C. disseminated intravascular coagulopathy. | **T** | Thrombocytopenia and FDP-induced platelet dysfunction. |
| D. antiphospholipid syndrome. | **F** | Not a bleeding disorder. |

> [!answer]
> **A T, B F, C T, D F**
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Bleeding time reflects **primary haemostasis**: prolonged in thrombocytopenia, platelet function defects, **vWD**, DIC and vascular disorders; normal in coagulation factor deficiencies (haemophilia, vitamin K deficiency).

## Simplified explanation

Bleeding time checks platelets and vessels. It is long in vWD and DIC, but normal in vitamin K deficiency and APS.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

Coagulation factors that may present in serum includes factor ...

A. II.
B. VI.
C. VII.
D. X.
answer:
| Option | T/F | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A. II. | **F** | Prothrombin is consumed during clotting. |
| B. VI. | **F** | Factor VI does not exist (it was found to be Va). |
| C. VII. | **T** | Not consumed. |
| D. X. | **T** | Present in serum. |

> [!answer]
> **A F, B F, C T, D T**
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Serum lacks the factors consumed by clotting: **fibrinogen, II, V, VIII, XIII**. Serum retains **VII, IX, X, XI, XII**. 'Factor VI' is obsolete (activated factor V).

## Simplified explanation

Serum still has factors VII and X; prothrombin is used up, and factor VI doesn't exist.
hint: Consumed: I, II, V, VIII, XIII.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

Causes of thrombocytosis include(s) ...

A. haemolysis.
B. splenectomy.
C. iron deficiency anaemia.
D. postpartum haemorrhage.
answer:
| Option | T/F | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A. haemolysis. | **T** | Reactive thrombocytosis follows haemolysis. |
| B. splenectomy. | **T** | Loss of the splenic platelet pool. |
| C. iron deficiency anaemia. | **T** | Common reactive cause. |
| D. postpartum haemorrhage. | **T** | Acute blood loss → reactive thrombocytosis. |

> [!answer]
> **A T, B T, C T, D T**
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Reactive thrombocytosis (raised TPO/IL-6 drive): iron deficiency, **haemorrhage** (including postpartum), **haemolysis**, **splenectomy**, infection, inflammation, malignancy, recovery from marrow suppression. Primary: myeloproliferative neoplasms.

## Simplified explanation

Bleeding, haemolysis, iron deficiency and removal of the spleen can all raise the platelet count.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

Mrs Akwartey has a requisition for the following laboratory testing: Blood culture, renal function test, coagulation screen, full blood count. The best order to fill the tubes if you were using syringe and needle system include ...

A. Blood culture, coagulation screen tube, full blood count tube, and renal function tube respectively
B. Blood culture, renal function tube, coagulation screen tube, and full blood count tube respectively
C. Blood culture, coagulation screen tube, renal function tube, and full blood count tubes respectively
D. Coagulation screen tube, blood culture tube, renal function tube and full blood count respectively
answer:
| Option | T/F | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A. Blood culture, coagulation screen tube, full blood count tube, and renal function tube respectively | **F** | EDTA (FBC) must come after the serum tube to avoid EDTA carry-over (falsely high K⁺, low Ca²⁺). |
| B. Blood culture, renal function tube, coagulation screen tube, and full blood count tube respectively | **F** | The citrate (coagulation) tube should precede serum tubes, whose clot activator can affect clotting tests. |
| C. Blood culture, coagulation screen tube, renal function tube, and full blood count tubes respectively | **T** | Matches the recommended order of draw. |
| D. Coagulation screen tube, blood culture tube, renal function tube and full blood count respectively | **F** | Blood culture (sterile) is always first. |

> [!answer]
> **A F, B F, C T, D F**
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

CLSI order of draw (also applied when transferring from a syringe): **blood culture → citrate (coagulation) → serum (plain/gel; renal function) → heparin → EDTA (FBC) → fluoride/oxalate**. This prevents microbial contamination of cultures and additive carry-over (clot activator into citrate, EDTA into chemistry tubes).

## Simplified explanation

Blood culture first, then the coagulation tube, then the serum (renal) tube, and EDTA (FBC) last.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

Mr Akuoko has been booked for coagulation screen test at 7 am in your laboratory. He woke up at 6:30 am that day and fearing that he might be held up in traffic, he decided to jog to your facility for the coagulation screen. He reached your facility at 6:59 am just as his name was called by the phlebotomist. If his sample was drawn immediately, the effects on his results includes ...

A. Increased factor VIII levels
B. Reduced fibrinogen levels
C. Increased platelet count
D. Increased fibrinolysis
answer:
| Option | T/F | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A. Increased factor VIII levels | **T** | Exercise releases FVIII/vWF from endothelium (adrenaline effect). |
| B. Reduced fibrinogen levels | **F** | Fibrinogen is not reduced by brief exercise. |
| C. Increased platelet count | **T** | Adrenaline releases splenic platelets. |
| D. Increased fibrinolysis | **T** | Exercise releases tPA. |

> [!answer]
> **A T, B F, C T, D T**
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Strenuous exercise and stress (adrenaline) acutely raise **FVIII and vWF**, **tPA** (enhanced fibrinolysis) and the **platelet count** (splenic release), and can shorten the APTT. Patients should rest ~20–30 minutes before sampling for haemostasis tests.

## Simplified explanation

Jogging raises factor VIII, platelets and clot-dissolving tPA for a while, so he should have rested before the blood draw.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

Platelet-rich plasma is required for ...

A. APTT assay
B. Platelet function assay
C. PT test
D. TT test
answer:
| Option | T/F | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A. APTT assay | **F** | Uses platelet-poor plasma. |
| B. Platelet function assay | **T** | Light transmission aggregometry uses PRP. |
| C. PT test | **F** | Uses platelet-poor plasma. |
| D. TT test | **F** | Uses platelet-poor plasma. |

> [!answer]
> **A F, B T, C F, D F**
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**PRP** (low-speed centrifugation ~150–200 g for 10–15 min) is used for **platelet aggregation studies** (light transmission aggregometry with ADP, collagen, adrenaline, arachidonic acid, ristocetin). Clotting tests (PT, APTT, TT, fibrinogen) use **PPP** (<10 × 10⁹/L platelets).

## Simplified explanation

Only platelet function tests need platelet-rich plasma; clotting tests use platelet-poor plasma.
hint: Which test studies the platelets themselves?

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

Platelet dense granules contain(s) ...

A. ATP
B. ADP
C. Factor V
D. Platelet factor 4
answer:
| Option | T/F | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A. ATP | **T** | Dense granule nucleotide. |
| B. ADP | **T** | Dense granule agonist. |
| C. Factor V | **F** | In α-granules. |
| D. Platelet factor 4 | **F** | In α-granules. |

> [!answer]
> **A T, B T, C F, D F**
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**Dense (δ) granules**: ADP, ATP, Ca²⁺, serotonin, pyrophosphate. **α-granules**: fibrinogen, vWF, factor V, PF4, β-thromboglobulin, PDGF, P-selectin.

## Simplified explanation

Dense granules hold ADP, ATP, calcium and serotonin; factor V and PF4 are in α-granules.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

The laboratory findings in Glanzmann's thrombasthenia include(s) ...

A. Prolonged APTT
B. Prolonged bleeding time
C. Abnormal clot retraction
D. Elevated fibrin split products
answer:
| Option | T/F | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A. Prolonged APTT | **F** | Coagulation factors are normal. |
| B. Prolonged bleeding time | **T** | Platelets cannot aggregate. |
| C. Abnormal clot retraction | **T** | GPIIb/IIIa is needed for clot retraction. |
| D. Elevated fibrin split products | **F** | Not a feature. |

> [!answer]
> **A F, B T, C T, D F**
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**Glanzmann thrombasthenia** (autosomal recessive, absent/defective **GPIIb/IIIa**, αIIbβ3): normal platelet count and morphology, **prolonged bleeding time/PFA closure**, **absent aggregation with all agonists except ristocetin**, **impaired clot retraction**; normal PT/APTT.

## Simplified explanation

Without GPIIb/IIIa platelets can't stick together or retract the clot, so bleeding time is long but clotting times are normal.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

In Bernard-Soulier syndrome ...

A. Von Willebrand factor is deficient
B. GpIIbIIIa is absent on platelet
C. Giant platelets are abundant on peripheral blood smear
D. Thrombocytopenia is a common finding
answer:
| Option | T/F | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A. Von Willebrand factor is deficient | **F** | vWF is normal; its receptor is missing. |
| B. GpIIbIIIa is absent on platelet | **F** | **GPIb-IX-V** is absent. |
| C. Giant platelets are abundant on peripheral blood smear | **T** | Characteristic giant platelets. |
| D. Thrombocytopenia is a common finding | **T** | Usually mild-moderate. |

> [!answer]
> **A F, B F, C T, D T**
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**Bernard-Soulier syndrome** (autosomal recessive): deficiency of **GPIb-IX-V** (vWF receptor) → defective adhesion; **thrombocytopenia with giant platelets**, prolonged bleeding time, **absent ristocetin-induced aggregation not corrected by normal plasma**, normal aggregation with ADP/collagen/adrenaline.

## Simplified explanation

BSS platelets lack the vWF receptor (GPIb), are few and giant.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

The physiological effects of thrombin include ...

A. Increased platelet aggregation
B. Activation of protein C
C. Degradation of factor Va and VIIIa
D. Enhanced clot retraction
answer:
| Option | T/F | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A. Increased platelet aggregation | **T** | Potent platelet agonist via PAR-1/PAR-4. |
| B. Activation of protein C | **T** | Thrombin bound to thrombomodulin activates protein C. |
| C. Degradation of factor Va and VIIIa | **F** | Thrombin **activates** V and VIII; degradation is done by activated protein C. |
| D. Enhanced clot retraction | **T** | Thrombin-activated platelets drive clot retraction. |

> [!answer]
> **A T, B T, C F, D T**
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Thrombin: converts fibrinogen → fibrin; activates **V, VIII, XI, XIII**; activates **platelets** (PAR-1/4) → aggregation, secretion, **clot retraction**; bound to **thrombomodulin** it activates **protein C** (which degrades Va/VIIIa) and TAFI. It also stimulates endothelium.

## Simplified explanation

Thrombin makes platelets clump and pull the clot tight and, with thrombomodulin, switches on protein C. It activates (not degrades) factors V and VIII.
hint: Thrombin is both pro- and anticoagulant.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

Transglutaminase ("transaminase" on the paper) coagulation factors includes ...

A. I
B. IX
C. X
D. XIII
answer:
| Option | T/F | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A. I | **F** | Fibrinogen is a substrate, not an enzyme. |
| B. IX | **F** | A serine protease. |
| C. X | **F** | A serine protease. |
| D. XIII | **T** | Factor XIIIa is a transglutaminase that cross-links fibrin. |

> [!answer]
> **A F, B F, C F, D T**
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Most activated clotting factors (II, VII, IX, X, XI, XII) are **serine proteases**; **FXIIIa** is a **transglutaminase** that forms covalent γ-glutamyl-ε-lysyl cross-links between fibrin monomers (and binds α2-antiplasmin to fibrin), stabilising the clot.

## Simplified explanation

Factor XIII is the only transglutaminase; it cross-links fibrin.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

Effects of aspirin on coagulation cascade include ...

A. Prolonged bleeding time
B. Impaired clot retraction
C. Prolonged thrombin time
D. Shortened APTT
answer:
| Option | T/F | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A. Prolonged bleeding time | **T** | Irreversible COX-1 inhibition blocks thromboxane A₂. |
| B. Impaired clot retraction | **F** | Clot retraction depends on GPIIb/IIIa and is normal with aspirin. |
| C. Prolonged thrombin time | **F** | Coagulation tests are unaffected. |
| D. Shortened APTT | **F** | Unaffected. |

> [!answer]
> **A T, B F, C F, D F**
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Aspirin acetylates platelet **COX-1** irreversibly for the platelet's lifespan (7–10 days), abolishing **TXA₂** synthesis: prolonged bleeding time/PFA, reduced aggregation to arachidonic acid and collagen (and secondary-wave ADP). PT, APTT, TT and clot retraction are normal.

## Simplified explanation

Aspirin stops platelets making thromboxane, so bleeding time is longer; clotting tests and clot retraction are unaffected.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

The laboratory findings in von Willebrand disease includes ...

A. Prolonged bleeding time
B. Failure of platelet aggregation with ristocetin
C. Prolonged APTT
D. Prolonged PT
answer:
| Option | T/F | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A. Prolonged bleeding time | **T** | Defective platelet adhesion. |
| B. Failure of platelet aggregation with ristocetin | **T** | Ristocetin-induced agglutination needs vWF. |
| C. Prolonged APTT | **T** | Low FVIII (vWF carries and protects FVIII). |
| D. Prolonged PT | **F** | Extrinsic pathway unaffected. |

> [!answer]
> **A T, B T, C T, D F**
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

vWD: **prolonged bleeding time/PFA-100**, reduced vWF antigen and activity (ristocetin cofactor), **reduced RIPA**, low **FVIII** → **prolonged APTT** (may be normal in mild type 1); PT normal; platelet count normal (low in type 2B).

## Simplified explanation

vWD affects platelet sticking (long bleeding time, poor ristocetin response) and lowers factor VIII (long APTT); PT is normal.
hint: vWF has two jobs: platelet adhesion and carrying FVIII.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

The anti-thrombogenic properties of endothelial cells include ...

A. Production of ADPase
B. Production of prostacyclin
C. Production of nitric oxide
D. Production of thromboxane A₂
answer:
| Option | T/F | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A. Production of ADPase | **T** | CD39 degrades ADP. |
| B. Production of prostacyclin | **T** | PGI₂ inhibits platelets and dilates vessels. |
| C. Production of nitric oxide | **T** | NO inhibits platelet adhesion/aggregation. |
| D. Production of thromboxane A₂ | **F** | TXA₂ is a platelet product that promotes aggregation. |

> [!answer]
> **A T, B T, C T, D F**
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Intact endothelium is anti-thrombotic: **PGI₂**, **NO**, **ecto-ADPase (CD39)**, heparan sulphate (enhances antithrombin), **thrombomodulin** (protein C activation), TFPI, and **tPA**. When damaged it becomes prothrombotic: vWF, tissue factor, PAI-1.

## Simplified explanation

Healthy vessel lining makes ADPase, prostacyclin and nitric oxide to stop clotting; thromboxane comes from platelets and promotes clotting.
hint: TXA₂ is the odd one out.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

Platelets expresses ...

A. MHC I
B. MHC II
C. ABO antigens
D. Rh antigens
answer:
| Option | T/F | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A. MHC I | **T** | HLA class I is present on platelets. |
| B. MHC II | **F** | Not expressed. |
| C. ABO antigens | **T** | ABH antigens are present. |
| D. Rh antigens | **F** | Rh is erythroid-specific. |

> [!answer]
> **A T, B F, C T, D F**
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Platelets carry **HLA class I**, **ABH** and platelet-specific **HPA** antigens, but not HLA class II or Rh. HLA class I antibodies cause platelet refractoriness.

## Simplified explanation

Platelets carry HLA class I and ABO, not class II or Rh.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

Platelet aggregating agents include ...

A. ATP
B. Serotonin
C. Prostacyclin
D. ADP
answer:
| Option | T/F | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A. ATP | **F** | ATP is not an aggregating agent (it antagonises the ADP receptor). |
| B. Serotonin | **T** | A weak agonist that amplifies aggregation. |
| C. Prostacyclin | **F** | An inhibitor of aggregation. |
| D. ADP | **T** | A key agonist (P2Y1/P2Y12). |

> [!answer]
> **A F, B T, C F, D T**
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Platelet agonists: **ADP**, thrombin, collagen, TXA₂, adrenaline, **serotonin** (weak), arachidonic acid, PAF. Inhibitors: **prostacyclin**, NO, ADPase; ATP is a competitive antagonist at P2Y receptors.

## Simplified explanation

ADP and serotonin promote platelet clumping; prostacyclin and ATP don't.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

The laboratory findings in haemophilia A includes ...

A. Prolonged bleeding time
B. Prolonged APTT
C. Prolonged PT
D. Prolonged TT
answer:
| Option | T/F | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A. Prolonged bleeding time | **F** | Platelet function is normal. |
| B. Prolonged APTT | **T** | FVIII is in the intrinsic pathway. |
| C. Prolonged PT | **F** | Extrinsic pathway intact. |
| D. Prolonged TT | **F** | Fibrinogen conversion is normal. |

> [!answer]
> **A F, B T, C F, D F**
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Haemophilia A (X-linked FVIII deficiency): **isolated prolonged APTT** that corrects on 1:1 mixing, **low FVIII:C**, normal PT, TT, bleeding time, platelet count and vWF.

## Simplified explanation

Haemophilia A only lengthens the APTT.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

In haemophilia B ...

A. Abnormal patient PT corrects with 1:1 mix with normal plasma
B. Abnormal patient APTT corrects with 1:1 mix with normal plasma
C. Abnormal patient APTT does not correct with 1:1 mix with normal plasma
D. Patients are managed with recombinant VIII when bleeding occurs
answer:
| Option | T/F | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A. Abnormal patient PT corrects with 1:1 mix with normal plasma | **F** | The PT is **normal** in haemophilia B. |
| B. Abnormal patient APTT corrects with 1:1 mix with normal plasma | **T** | Factor deficiency corrects on mixing. |
| C. Abnormal patient APTT does not correct with 1:1 mix with normal plasma | **F** | Non-correction indicates an inhibitor. |
| D. Patients are managed with recombinant VIII when bleeding occurs | **F** | They need **factor IX** concentrate. |

> [!answer]
> **A F, B T, C F, D F**
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Haemophilia B (Christmas disease) = X-linked **factor IX** deficiency: prolonged APTT that **corrects with normal plasma**, normal PT, low FIX assay; treated with recombinant/plasma-derived **FIX** (or gene therapy).

## Simplified explanation

In haemophilia B only the APTT is long, it corrects on mixing, and treatment is factor IX.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

Abnormal platelet function leads to ...

A. Mucousal bleeding
B. Haemarrthrosis
C. Haematoma
D. Menorrhagia
answer:
| Option | T/F | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A. Mucousal bleeding | **T** | Epistaxis, gum bleeding: typical of platelet disorders. |
| B. Haemarrthrosis | **F** | Typical of coagulation factor deficiency (haemophilia). |
| C. Haematoma | **F** | Deep muscle haematomas suggest coagulation factor deficiency. |
| D. Menorrhagia | **T** | Common in platelet disorders and vWD. |

> [!answer]
> **A T, B F, C F, D T**
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**Primary haemostasis** defects (platelets, vWF) give **mucocutaneous** bleeding: petechiae, purpura, epistaxis, gum bleeding, **menorrhagia**, prolonged bleeding from cuts. **Coagulation factor** defects give **deep** bleeding: haemarthroses, muscle haematomas, delayed bleeding after trauma.

## Simplified explanation

Platelet problems cause surface bleeding (nose, gums, heavy periods); joint and muscle bleeds point to factor deficiencies.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

Factor VIII ...

A. Gene is on chromosome 9
B. Stabilises vWF
C. Produced in endothelial cells
D. Is synthesised exclusively in the liver
answer:
| Option | T/F | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A. Gene is on chromosome 9 | **F** | The F8 gene is on the **X chromosome** (Xq28). |
| B. Stabilises vWF | **F** | It is the other way round: **vWF stabilises FVIII**. |
| C. Produced in endothelial cells | **T** | Mainly liver sinusoidal endothelial cells. |
| D. Is synthesised exclusively in the liver | **F** | Produced by endothelial cells (liver sinusoids and elsewhere). |

> [!answer]
> **A F, B F, C T, D F**
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

FVIII is encoded on **Xq28** and synthesised mainly by **liver sinusoidal endothelial cells** (and other endothelia). In plasma it circulates bound to **vWF**, which protects it from proteolysis (half-life ~12 h vs ~2 h without vWF). Hence FVIII is low in severe vWD.

## Simplified explanation

Factor VIII comes from the X chromosome, is made by endothelial cells, and is protected by vWF.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

Antithrombin III inactivates ...

A. IIa
B. VIIIa
C. Xa
D. XIIa
answer:
| Option | T/F | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A. IIa | **T** | Thrombin is the main target. |
| B. VIIIa | **F** | VIIIa is a cofactor inactivated by activated protein C. |
| C. Xa | **T** | A major target (basis of LMWH/fondaparinux action). |
| D. XIIa | **T** | AT also inhibits XIIa, XIa and IXa. |

> [!answer]
> **A T, B F, C T, D T**
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**Antithrombin** is a serpin that inactivates the serine proteases **thrombin, Xa**, IXa, XIa, **XIIa** (and VIIa–TF), greatly accelerated by heparin/heparan sulphate. Cofactors **Va and VIIIa** are inactivated by **activated protein C** with protein S.

## Simplified explanation

Antithrombin blocks the protease factors (IIa, Xa, XIIa...). Factor VIIIa is switched off by protein C instead.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

Reasons for rejecting samples meant for coagulation studies includes ...

A. Tubes that are 92% filled as per the anticoagulant it contains
B. haemolysed sample
C. if 2.7 ml blood is added to a tube with 0.3 ml anticoagulant
D. if the ratio of blood to anticoagulant is 1:9
answer:
| Option | T/F | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A. Tubes that are 92% filled as per the anticoagulant it contains | **F** | ≥90% fill is acceptable. |
| B. haemolysed sample | **T** | Haemolysis activates coagulation and interferes with optical detection. |
| C. if 2.7 ml blood is added to a tube with 0.3 ml anticoagulant | **F** | That is the correct 9:1 ratio. |
| D. if the ratio of blood to anticoagulant is 1:9 | **T** | Grossly excessive anticoagulant (should be 9:1). |

> [!answer]
> **A F, B T, C F, D T**
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Reject coagulation samples that are **under-filled (<90%)**, clotted, **haemolysed**, in the wrong tube/ratio, mislabelled, or too old. The correct ratio is **9 blood : 1 citrate**.

## Simplified explanation

Haemolysed samples and a reversed 1:9 ratio must be rejected; a 92% fill and 2.7 + 0.3 ml are fine.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

Platelet GpIIbIIIa is a receptor for ...

A. Fibronectin
B. Fibrinogen
C. Factor V
D. Von Willebrand factor
answer:
| Option | T/F | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A. Fibronectin | **T** | An RGD-containing ligand. |
| B. Fibrinogen | **T** | The principal ligand for aggregation. |
| C. Factor V | **F** | Not a GPIIb/IIIa ligand. |
| D. Von Willebrand factor | **T** | Binds activated GPIIb/IIIa (as well as GPIb). |

> [!answer]
> **A T, B T, C F, D T**
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Activated **αIIbβ3 (GPIIb/IIIa)** binds RGD/KQAGDV-containing adhesive proteins: **fibrinogen** (main), **vWF**, **fibronectin**, vitronectin, bridging platelets in aggregation. GPIb-IX-V binds vWF for adhesion; GPVI/GPIa-IIa bind collagen.

## Simplified explanation

GPIIb/IIIa binds fibrinogen, vWF and fibronectin, not factor V.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

Prothrombin group of coagulation factors include ...

A. VII
B. IX
C. X
D. XII
answer:
| Option | T/F | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A. VII | **T** | Vitamin K-dependent. |

The prothrombin group is II, VII, IX and X (vitamin K-dependent); XII is a contact factor.

explanation:
## Advanced explanation

PT depends on factors VII, X, V, II and fibrinogen; IX and XII only affect the APTT.

B. Thrombocytopenia
C. Von Willebrand's disease

Liver disease, vWD and FVIII deficiency lengthen the APTT; low platelets don't.

FVIII is X-linked and unstable; its deficiency is haemophilia A with a long APTT.

A. PT is normal in haemophilia A whereas PT is elevated in vWD

D. PT is prolonged in haemophilia A but normal in vWD

| B. APTT is normal in haemophilia A whereas APTT is reduced in vWD | **F** | APTT is prolonged in haemophilia A (and often in vWD). |

| D. PT is prolonged in haemophilia A but normal in vWD | **F** | PT is normal in both. |

explanation:
## Advanced explanation

The key difference is bleeding time: normal in haemophilia A, long in vWD.

Gut bacteria such as E. coli and Bacteroides make vitamin K; it is needed for II, VII, IX and X, not I or XIII.

B. Broad spectrum antibiotic therapy
C. Chronic diarrhoea

| C. Chronic diarrhoea | **T** | Malabsorption. |
| D. Inflammatory bowel disease | **T** | Malabsorption. |

> [!answer]

explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Causes of vitamin K deficiency: newborn, poor diet, **malabsorption** (biliary obstruction, coeliac disease, **IBD**, **chronic diarrhoea**, pancreatic insufficiency), **broad-spectrum antibiotics**, vitamin K antagonists (warfarin, rodenticides).

## Simplified explanation

Anything that blocks fat absorption or kills gut bacteria can cause vitamin K deficiency. All four are true.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

Vitamin K deficiency causes ...

A. PT elevation
B. APTT elevation
C. TT elevation
D. Prolonged bleeding time
answer:
| Option | T/F | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A. PT elevation | **T** | FVII has the shortest half-life, so PT rises first. |
| B. APTT elevation | **T** | IX, X, II deficiency. |
| C. TT elevation | **F** | Fibrinogen is not affected. |
| D. Prolonged bleeding time | **F** | Platelet function is normal. |

explanation:
## Advanced explanation

## Simplified explanation

PT and APTT get longer; TT and bleeding time stay normal.

Fibrinogen is an **acute-phase protein** (IL-6-induced): raised in inflammation, infection, malignancy, trauma/stress, **pregnancy**, oral contraceptives, smoking, **diabetes**, obesity and ageing; it is an independent cardiovascular risk factor and raises the ESR.

## Simplified explanation

Fibrinogen goes up with pregnancy, stress, diabetes and inflammation. All four are true.

body:
A randomly selected patient sample was run (20X) through the Sysmex haematology analyzer at the Cape Coast teaching hospital laboratory. The values for the MCV (fL) were:

92.6, 91.5, 89.1, 93.5, 91.9, 90.7, 93.9, 92.7, 86.7, 87.5, 90.3, 94.4, 90.8, 88.0, 93.5, 95.6, 90.7, 91.6, 92.6, 90.3

Determine if the analyzer is in compliance given that the acceptable limits of coefficient of variation (CV) for MCV is 4 – 5%.
answer:
1. **Mean** = Σx ÷ n = 1827.9 ÷ 20 = **91.40 fL**
2. **SD** = √[Σ(x − x̄)² ÷ (n − 1)] ≈ **2.35 fL**
3. **CV** = SD ÷ mean × 100 = 2.35 ÷ 91.40 × 100 ≈ **2.6%**

The CV (≈2.6%) is **below** the acceptable limit of 4–5%, so the analyser's precision is acceptable: it is **in compliance**.

> [!answer]
> Mean 91.4 fL, SD 2.35 fL, CV ≈ 2.6% (< 4–5%): compliant.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Within-run **precision (repeatability)** is assessed by analysing one sample many times and calculating the CV, which expresses SD as a percentage of the mean. A CV within the allowable limit indicates acceptable imprecision; accuracy (bias) needs calibrators or reference methods.

## Simplified explanation

Average the 20 values (91.4), work out the spread (SD 2.35) and divide: CV is about 2.6%, inside the 4–5% limit, so the analyser passes.

body:
The head of the haematology unit at Ewim Polyclinic picked random patient sample daily and run it in duplicate on the Mindray haematology analyzer over the course of 20 consecutive days. The results of the MCV (1st run / 2nd run) were:

| Day | 1st | 2nd | Day | 1st | 2nd |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 92.6 | 92.6 | 11 | 90.3 | 90.0 |
| 2 | 91.5 | 91.9 | 12 | 94.4 | 94.1 |
| 3 | 89.1 | 85.0 | 13 | 90.8 | 90.3 |
| 4 | 93.5 | 92.1 | 14 | 88.0 | 86.9 |
| 5 | 91.9 | 90.1 | 15 | 93.5 | 92.5 |
| 6 | 90.7 | 92.1 | 16 | 95.6 | 95.6 |
| 7 | 93.9 | 92.5 | 17 | 90.7 | 90.6 |
| 8 | 92.7 | 92.7 | 18 | 91.6 | 91.1 |
| 9 | 86.7 | 87.0 | 19 | 92.6 | 93.0 |
| 10 | 87.5 | 85.9 | 20 | 90.3 | 89.5 |

Determine if the analyzer is working within the limits (acceptable CV for MCV 4–5%).
answer:
Use the **duplicate method**: SD = √(Σd² ÷ 2n), where d = difference between the paired runs and n = number of pairs.

1. Differences (1st − 2nd): 0, −0.4, 4.1, 1.4, 1.8, −1.4, 1.4, 0, −0.3, 1.6, 0.3, 0.3, 0.5, 1.1, 1.0, 0, 0.1, 0.5, −0.4, 0.8
2. **Σd² = 32.44**
3. SD = √(32.44 ÷ 40) ≈ **0.90 fL**
4. Mean of all 40 results ≈ **91.09 fL**
5. **CV** = 0.90 ÷ 91.09 × 100 ≈ **0.99%**

The CV (~1%) is well within the 4–5% limit, so the analyser is **working within limits**. (Day 3, with a 4.1 fL difference, is the largest discrepancy and is worth reviewing.)

> [!answer]
> Σd² = 32.44, SD ≈ 0.90 fL, CV ≈ 1%: within limits.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Duplicate testing of patient samples is a practical way to monitor **imprecision** without commercial controls; SD = √(Σd²/2n) estimates the analytical SD from paired results. Large individual differences (e.g. Day 3) may indicate mixing problems, clots or instrument faults.

## Simplified explanation

Find each pair's difference, square and add them (32.44); SD = √(32.44/40) ≈ 0.9 and CV ≈ 1%, well within limits.

body:
Patient Akwasi Mintah came to the laboratory unit for a coagulation screening assay. The attending clinician decided that the result was at "variance" with the patient clinical presentation and therefore sent the patient back to the laboratory for a repeat of the coagulation screen the following day. The two results are tabulated below.

| Coagulation screen | Day 1 | Day 2 |
|---|---|---|
| PT (s) [ref 10–12] | 4 | 15 |
| APTT (s) [ref 26–40] | 6 | 30 |
| TT (s) [ref 15–19] | 8 | 18 |
| Platelet count (×10⁹/L) [ref 150–400] | 52.1 | 172.2 |

Supposing that the reagents were not expired and a citrated tube was used in both instances:

(I) State five (5) factors that could have led to these discrepant results.
(II) Explain how each of the factors stated in (I) would have contributed to the discrepancy in the results.
answer:
Day 1 shows impossibly **short** PT, APTT and TT with a **low platelet count**, typical of a **pre-activated/partially clotted sample**; Day 2 is plausible.

| Factor (I) | How it causes the discrepancy (II) |
|---|---|
| **Traumatic/difficult venepuncture** (prolonged tourniquet, probing) | Tissue factor from damaged tissue activates coagulation in the tube, shortening clotting times; platelets aggregate and are consumed |
| **Inadequate mixing / partially clotted sample** | Thrombin forms in the tube; activated factors shorten PT/APTT/TT and platelets are trapped in microclots |
| **Wrong blood:citrate ratio** (overfilled tube → too little citrate) | Insufficient anticoagulation allows activation and microclots |
| **Delay or improper storage** (e.g. refrigerated whole blood) | Cold activation of FVII and contact factors; platelet activation/clumping |
| **Haemolysis** | Released red cell phospholipid and ADP accelerate clotting and activate platelets |
| **Contamination/sample mix-up** (IV line, wrong patient, poor centrifugation) | Wrong or contaminated sample gives implausible results |

> [!answer]
> Day 1 = activated/partially clotted sample: e.g. traumatic venepuncture, poor mixing/microclots, wrong blood:citrate ratio, delayed or cold storage, haemolysis (or sample mix-up). These generate thrombin in vitro, shortening PT/APTT/TT and consuming platelets.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Most errors in coagulation testing are **pre-analytical**. Shortened clotting times are rarely real and usually indicate in-vitro activation. CLSI H21: 3.2% citrate, 9:1 ratio (≥90% fill), clean venepuncture, gentle inversion 3–4 times, processing within 1–4 h at room temperature, platelet-poor plasma, no refrigeration of whole blood for PT.

## Simplified explanation

The first sample was probably partly clotted (bad draw, poor mixing, wrong fill, old/cold or haemolysed sample). Clotting started in the tube, so times looked too short and platelets were used up.
hint: Short clotting times + low platelets = clotted sample.
